Chatbot Q&A — David West

> This document is the primary knowledge source for David's portfolio chatbot. Each question represents something a recruiter, hiring manager, or technical interviewer might ask the chatbot. David's answers are used by the RAG pipeline to generate accurate, grounded responses.
>
> Format: Answer each question in the first person ("I ..."). Be specific — include technologies, timeframes, outcomes, and concrete examples wherever possible. Vague answers produce vague chatbot responses.

About David

Above anything, I'm a husband and a father. I'm also a hard-working self starter who learns and adapts quickly and likes to be challenged.

father. I'm also a hard-working self starter who learns and adapts quickly and likes to be challenged. What is David's background?

AI & Machine Learning What is David's experience with machine learning?
During my time at Booz Allen, I frequently used different Optical Character Recognition (OCR) models to extract text from documents and images, including AWS Textract and Tesseract. Recently, I have been using a LLM approach to OCR to extract the relevant text, which has been more effective and accurate than traditional OCR methods, however it's confidence scores are not reliable compared to traditional models. So, I developed three classification models (logistic regression, random forest, and histogram gradient boosting machine) to predict the accuracy of the LLM approach using a human-validated dataset. I also developed a prototype isolation forest model to detect potential fraudulent financial activity. This was a prototype that wasn't pursed since there were common rule-based detection methods that sufficed. The simpler solution, is often the better one.

I initially experimented with classical per-series models like ARIMA before implementing a multi-horizon pooled forecasting model using LightGBM. The pipeline engineers lag and rolling features across thousands of names, backtests 5-year forecasts against historical baselines, and generates conformal prediction intervals to capture forecast uncertainty.

Does David use AI coding assistants?
Yes, I use AI coding assistants frequently to help me with my day to day work. At work, I utilize a government-approved version of Windsurf/Devin. At home, I use Antigravity and Claude Code. I also have experience using Cursor.

of Windsurf/Devin. At home, I use Antigravity and Claude Code. I also have experience using Cursor. How does David use AI coding assistants? I'm a fan of Matt Pocock's development workflow, "AI Skills for Real Engineers". I'll start by defining the problem statement and the desired outcome and provide any relevant context. Then I invoke the skill "grill-with-docs" which prompts the AI to "grill the user relentlessly about a plan, decision, or idea" and "build and sharpen a project's domain model". This entails a prolonged session of Q&A with the AI and updating the project's documentation to continue to build the context needed for this AI agent and future AI agents. I go back and forth with the AI agent through multiple rounds of questioning until I'm satisfied with the technical direction and we're both confident in the architectural design. After the design is settled, I'll invoke the skill "to-spec" to "turn the current conversation into a spec and publish it to the project issue tracker." I've recently been using GitHub actions as the issue tracker.

publish it to the project issue tracker." I've recently been using GitHub actions as the issue tracker. Then I invoke the skill "to-tickets" that breaks the spec into individual vertical slices of the problem and they get published to the issue tracker. After all the tickets are made, I create a new session and give the AI the spec and one vertical slice to complete and tell it use test driven development. If vertical slices are independent from each other, I can have the AI work on multiple vertical slices in parallel. I iterate until all vertical slices are complete and then have the AI create a pull request (PR). I then have an AI agent perform a review of the PR and mitigate any findings. Finally, I'll perform a manual review of the PR and perform any manual end-to-end testing that is needed. If everything is good, I merge to main. Using this workflow has been yielding high quality outputs and has allowed me to be more productive while still being in control of the overall direction of the project and understanding the technical architecture.

What projects has David built?
My featured projects span generative AI, time-series forecasting, RAG, and end-to-end machine learning. Key projects include the Baby Names Explorer with pooled LightGBM time-series forecasting and a text-to-SQL chatbot, a Nietzsche Persona Chatbot built on RAG over philosophical texts, an AI Music Generator running ACE-Step on serverless Modal GPUs, a supervised Diamond Price Prediction model, and this portfolio itself, which features an evaluated RAG retrieval pipeline in CI/CD. Professionally, I also lead Data ReconnAIssance™ at Booz Allen, a production-deployed, IL5-compliant Document AI extraction system for governement data like engineering drawings.

production-deployed, IL5-compliant Document AI extraction system for governement data like engineering drawings. Which of David's projects best demonstrates his AI engineering skills? My most recent project for Arlington National Cemetery required the extraction of text from old paper records of interment to provide an automated quality check of their existing database of records. Over 260k records were processed with LLMs in progressively bigger batches, with iterative improvements in between batches. Scalability was obtained by creating a parallelized, serverless AWS architecture composed of Bedrock Data Automation (BDA), DynamoDB, Lambda, SQS, SNS, CloudWatch, and more. Accuracy of extractions was determined with human-in-the-loop verification which created a dataset to develop an accuracy prediction model to identify likely errors in future extractions and prioritize human review accordingly. An internal app was developed to run these batch jobs, monitor the success rate, and have human-in-the-loop review of the records.

to run these batch jobs, monitor the success rate, and have human-in-the-loop review of the records. The internal app's framework was built using React, FastAPI, and Chainguard Docker images and was deployed to an EKS cluster I created for the project. All this architecture was built in accordance with CMMC Level 2 compliance. Finally, an open-source LLM approach using Ollama and Gemma4 is currently being evaluated for this project to normalize some of the LLM extractions. Specifically, determining what is the first, middle, and last name for a name that is extracted in various formats (e.g., "John Jacob Smith" vs "Smith, John Jacob" vs "Smith, J. Jacob" vs "Smith, Jacob J.").

Yes, both in enterprise defense environments and in public web applications. For the Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center (AFNWC), I deployed an enterprise Document AI pipeline into an Impact Level 5 (IL5) AWS GovCloud environment. The system processes complex engineering drawings using Bedrock and a serverless AWS backend (Lambda, SQS, SNS, DynamoDB, CloudWatch) to automatically build Bills of Materials (BOMs) and detect hazardous materials. I collaborated with a Cloud Ops team to deploy the containerized web services (React, FastAPI, Chainguard Docker images) onto their managed EKS cluster using Azure DevOps pipelines. As part of rigorous DevSecOps compliance, I mitigated security findings from static code analysis (SonarQube) and container vulnerability scanning (Grype and Syft).

findings from static code analysis (SonarQube) and container vulnerability scanning (Grype and Syft). In addition to defense systems, I have deployed several public-facing AI apps to production—including a text-to-music generation platform running serverless GPU inference on Modal with a FastAPI backend on Railway and Next.js on Vercel, as well as this portfolio's evaluated RAG chatbot.

FastAPI backend on Railway and Next.js on Vercel, as well as this portfolio's evaluated RAG chatbot. What is the most technically complex thing David has built?
The most technically complex systems I've built are my enterprise Document AI pipelines for high-stakes unstructured documents, such as military engineering drawings and historical records. Engineering drawings in particular present extreme complexity: standard models struggle with mixed visual schematics, rotated text, and nested tabular callouts. I solved this by building hybrid architectures that fuse computer vision (AWS Textract), deterministic rule-based NLP (regex for hierarchical Bill of Materials and hazardous material extraction), and multimodal LLMs. I coupled this algorithmic pipeline with event-driven serverless cloud backends (Lambda, SQS, DynamoDB, Bedrock) capable of processing hundreds of thousands of records, integrated active-learning error prediction models to prioritize human review, and deployed full-stack review tools to Kubernetes under strict DoD compliance.

prioritize human review, and deployed full-stack review tools to Kubernetes under strict DoD compliance. Has David built any full-stack AI applications?
Yes, I have built and deployed multiple full-stack AI applications across both enterprise defense and public projects. My full-stack AI projects feature modern TypeScript/React and Next.js frontends paired with containerized FastAPI backends and dedicated AI inference layers. For example, my AI Music Generator uses Next.js with WaveSurfer.js on the frontend, a stateless FastAPI proxy on Railway handling rate limiting and validation, and serverless GPU workers on Modal executing ACE-Step diffusion inference with async job polling. In my enterprise work, I designed and containerized a full-stack internal review platform using React and FastAPI, deploying it to AWS EKS with event-driven Bedrock processing for human-in-the-loop document validation. I also built the Baby Names Explorer, which connects a Next.js UI to a FastAPI service running pooled LightGBM time-series forecasting and Groq text-to-SQL generation.

to a FastAPI service running pooled LightGBM time-series forecasting and Groq text-to-SQL generation. Does David have any open source contributions or public projects?

On the open-source front, I contributed serverless GPU deployment support on Modal to ACE-Step 1.5, a leading open-source music foundation model, allowing developers to run on-demand, cold-start optimized diffusion inference without paying for idle GPU instances. Furthermore, all of my personal projects—including the AI Music Generator, Baby Names Explorer, Nietzsche Chatbot, and this Portfolio—are publicly open-sourced on my GitHub (github.com/dwest1507). Rather than treating personal work as quick prototypes, I build my public repositories with production-grade software engineering practices, including comprehensive automated test suites, GitHub Actions CI/CD gates, Architectural Decision Records (ADRs), and containerized deployments.

This Portfolio Chatbot How does this chatbot work?
This chatbot is a full-stack Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system built to answer questions accurately and honestly about my background. When you submit a question in the Next.js chat widget, the request proxies to a Python FastAPI backend. The backend queries a pre-indexed corpus of my resume, project write-ups, and background documents using an evaluation-selected retrieval pipeline. Rather than guessing retrieval parameters, I built an automated evaluation harness that benchmarks multiple retrieval configurations—including dense semantic search (FAISS with all-mpnet-base-v2), lexical keyword search (BM25), and cross-encoder re-ranking—against a labeled golden dataset in CI/CD, automatically shipping whichever configuration performs best. The top-scoring passages are then injected into a strictly grounded system prompt and sent to an LLM hosted on Groq for low-latency streaming inference directly back to your browser.

The chatbot is built on a modern, decoupled full-stack architecture. The frontend is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS, providing an interactive interface that consumes streaming responses via Server-Sent Events (SSE). The backend is a Python FastAPI service using Pydantic for validation, SlowAPI for rate limiting, and Uvicorn for asynchronous serving. For retrieval, the production runtime uses a fast, lightweight BM25 keyword index (rank-bm25), while the development and evaluation pipeline leverages sentence-transformers (all-mpnet-base-v2, ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2) and faiss-cpu. LLM inference is handled via Groq's high-speed API for ultra-low latency. The application is containerized with Docker—engineered to separate heavy ML dependencies so the production image remains under 550MB—and continuously validated via GitHub Actions CI/CD before deploying to Vercel and Railway.

Evaluation Has David done evaluation work on AI systems?
Yes — the chatbot you're talking to is the example I'd point at. I built a retrieval evaluation suite for it: a golden set of labelled questions split into development and held-out portions, five retrieval configurations scored against identical labels, and a CI gate that fails the build if retrieval quality regresses. The results are published on the portfolio project page, including the ones that were unflattering. The evaluation is also what chose the configuration that ships.

including the ones that were unflattering. The evaluation is also what chose the configuration that ships. How does David evaluate a RAG system?
I start by deciding what "good" means before measuring anything. For retrieval I label a set of realistic questions with the phrases a correct answer has to be grounded in, then score configurations on hit rate, recall, MRR, and nDCG. I gate CI on hit@k specifically, because that's what determines whether the model can answer at all — the other metrics are informative but make poor gates. I set thresholds below measured performance as regression floors, never as targets, because tuning until a threshold is cleared is just fitting to your own test set. I also hold back a portion of the labelled questions and never look at them while making a decision, so the numbers I publish aren't the numbers something was tuned against.

them while making a decision, so the numbers I publish aren't the numbers something was tuned against. Why does David label relevance by phrase instead of by document?
Because the corpus gets re-split every time a source document changes. Labels tied to a chunk's identity are invalidated on every rebuild, so they rot faster than you can maintain them. Phrases survive re-chunking, which is what makes the labelled set an asset instead of a chore.

them. Phrases survive re-chunking, which is what makes the labelled set an asset instead of a chore. What has David's evaluation work actually found?
Two real bugs that no test caught, and one wrong architecture. A tokenizer mismatch between index-time and query-time was silently destroying keyword recall — fixing it moved MRR from 0.745 to 0.892. A rank-fusion constant taken from a paper was being used at the wrong scale, which meant one of the two retrievers could never contribute a result; fusion was running, passing its tests, and doing nothing. In both of those cases every component behaved exactly as specified and only a metric moved. The third finding was bigger: the hybrid semantic-plus-keyword pipeline with a cross-encoder lost to plain keyword search on every metric, so I deleted it rather than tuned it.

a cross-encoder lost to plain keyword search on every metric, so I deleted it rather than tuned it. Does David use evaluation results to change what he builds? That's the entire point of collecting them. The eval showed that plain keyword search was beating my hybrid pipeline with a cross-encoder on every metric, which is not the result I wanted after building it. Rather than quietly retuning a fusion weight to make the number look better, I added a configuration that asked the actual question — keyword results fed straight to the cross-encoder, with no semantic search at all — and it beat the full pipeline. Then the cross-encoder failed the same test against keyword search alone. So the fix was to delete architecture rather than add it: production now runs keyword search only, which cut the backend from 87 production dependencies to 40 and the deployed container image from 17.2GB to 544MB — most of that being the CUDA libraries that torch pulls in behind the embedding model, shipped into a container with no GPU.

the project page recording what each measurement showed and what changed in the code because of it. Why doesn't David's chatbot use semantic or vector search?
It did, and the evaluation said it wasn't earning its place on this corpus. Retrieval is BM25 keyword search over a stemmed, stopword-filtered index. I'm not claiming semantic search is a bad idea in general — this corpus is written as anticipated questions and answers, which is exactly the condition that flatters keyword matching, and I expect that to stop being true as the corpus grows. The semantic and re-ranking configurations are still implemented and still measured on every evaluation run, so when the answer flips it'll be a measurement that tells me, not a rebuild.

every evaluation run, so when the answer flips it'll be a measurement that tells me, not a rebuild. How does David keep published metrics from going stale?
The numbers aren't written by hand anywhere. CI runs the evaluation, writes the results to a file, and commits it; the project page and the repository docs both render from that file. Even the sentence comparing the shipped configuration to the best-scoring one is generated from the data, so the write-up can't drift into claiming something the measurements no longer support.

What has David not measured yet?
Retrieval quality is only half of a RAG system's behaviour. Generation faithfulness — does the answer stay inside the retrieved context? — plus refusal behaviour on out-of-scope questions and adversarial robustness are all still unmeasured. I'd rather name those gaps than imply the evaluation covers more than it does.

Key Engineering Decisions

Technical Architecture

Key Engineering Decisions - Speculative GPU Prewarm (ADR 0001): Cold starting a multi-gigabyte diffusion model on serverless GPUs can take 30 to 45 seconds. By initiating prewarm on first user interaction rather than form submission, the GPU is warm before the user clicks generate. Heartbeats pause when the browser tab is hidden and terminate after a capped duration to strictly control cloud GPU costs. - Client-IP Rate Limiting: Rate limits are keyed strictly on client IP rather than session cookies. Because session cookies are client-supplied, rotating cookies previously minted fresh allowances; IP-based limiting provides robust abuse prevention across all endpoints. - HTTP/2 with httpx: The ACEStepClient is instantiated once during the FastAPI lifespan startup and shared across requests. Driving persistent HTTP/2 with httpx eliminates repeated TCP handshake overhead and multiplexes requests to Modal.

persistent HTTP/2 with httpx eliminates repeated TCP handshake overhead and multiplexes requests to Modal. - Production CI/CD & DevSecOps: Comprehensive automated GitHub Actions pipelines enforce code quality (Ruff, ESLint, Prettier, TypeScript verification), unit testing (Pytest and Vitest with uv caching), and automated security scanning including SAST (Semgrep, Bandit), secrets detection (Gitleaks), container vulnerability auditing (Trivy), and automated semantic releases via Release Please.

Baby Names Explorer is an interactive data application for exploring 145 years of US baby name trends from the Social Security Administration (1880–2024). You can browse the most popular names for any year, pull up the full history of any single name with a 5-year machine-learning popularity forecast with measured uncertainty bands and projected ranks, and ask questions about the entire dataset in plain English.

The project began as a single-file Streamlit app. It has since been rebuilt as a decoupled, production-grade system: a Next.js 16 frontend over a Python FastAPI backend, with reproducible data ingestion, an empirical ML forecasting pipeline, and automated CI/CD validation gates.

Data Pipeline & Database Architecture

ML forecasting pipeline, and automated CI/CD validation gates.

Data Pipeline & Database Architecture The SSA publishes baby name records as annual text files behind anti-bot protections. Ingestion is fully automated and reproducible via : it handles download automation, aggregates and cleans ~145 annual files, computes relative metrics ( share within sex/year, ), and builds a composite index  for zero-overhead streaming.

Relative metrics matter more than raw counts: a mid-century name given to 30,000 babies was a national phenomenon; the same count today in a much larger and more diverse birth pool represents a far smaller share.

The database is treated as a published build artifact rather than being checked into git:

- Observed records, canonical indexes, and precomputed forecast tables are generated via automated batch scripts.
- The artifact is validated by an automated deployment gate () before publication.
- At runtime, the FastAPI backend resolves  locally or downloads it from Hugging Face Hub, opening all connections in read-only mode ().

resolves  locally or downloads it from Hugging Face Hub, opening all connections in read-only mode (). Forecasting: From Per-Name ARIMA to Pooled LightGBM

The core forecasting challenge is projecting a name's popularity trajectory over a 5-year horizon ($h \in \{1..5\}$).

Why Per-Name ARIMA Was Replaced

The original prototype explored per-name ARIMA modeling, running ADF and KPSS stationarity tests to determine differencing orders and selecting orders via AICc. However, rigorous rolling-origin backtesting across historical decades revealed a structural limitation: with only 30 to 100 annual observations per series, individual series lack the statistical power to reliably satisfy stationarity or identify true ARIMA orders. While ARIMA performed moderately in the top 100 names (+0.161 skill), it produced negative skill outside the top 1,000 (–0.211 on ranks 1001–5000, –0.413 beyond 5000) — meaning visitors were receiving forecasts demonstrably worse than a flat-line naive baseline.

The Pooled Gradient-Boosted Model

receiving forecasts demonstrably worse than a flat-line naive baseline.

The Pooled Gradient-Boosted Model The solution was shifting to a pooled model: training across every eligible name's history simultaneously. A single LightGBM booster is trained per horizon ($h \in \{1..5\}$) over a rolling 40-origin training window:

- Target: Scale-free relative log growth $\log(y_{t+h} / y_t)$.
- Feature engineering: 13-feature base block including multi-horizon momentum (1/2/3/5/10-year growth), acceleration, historical volatility, popularity level, and distance/years from historical peaks and troughs.
- Sample weighting: $\text{share}^{0.5}$ weighting to prioritize names visitors search for without letting a few historical giants dominate the split criteria.

Post-Processing Stack

Direct booster outputs undergo a three-step sequential correction pipeline:

Post-Processing Stack

Direct booster outputs undergo a three-step sequential correction pipeline: 1. Growth capping: Path implied log-growth is clipped at the empirical 99.9th percentile of historical 5-year moves, preventing unbounded extrapolation on volatile low-volume names.
2. Path smoothing: An endpoint-preserving 3-point moving average over the log steps eliminates erratic year-over-year oscillations without altering the 5-year terminal projection.
3. Global reconciliation: Because popularity is a zero-sum share of total births within a sex, multiplicative scaling reconciles the slice total onto the origin year's observed sum.

Conformal Uncertainty Bands & Projected Ranks

the slice total onto the origin year's observed sum.

Conformal Uncertainty Bands & Projected Ranks - Conformal prediction bands: Rather than assuming theoretical Gaussian residuals, the 80% and 95% uncertainty intervals are derived from empirical residual quantiles stratified by popularity tier and volatility bin. A volatile breakout name receives an appropriately wider band than an entrenched classic at the same rank.
- Projected ranks: Each forecast point includes a projected rank computed against a frozen field of all recorded names at that origin, preventing rank distortions in the long tail.
- Deploy gate:  enforces that every published artifact beats the naive baseline across a 26-window backtest span, scoring positive skill across every tier (+0.374 in the top 100).

2. Resource-budgeted execution: Generated SQL is validated against strict keyword guards (allowing only  or  CTEs) and executed on a dedicated read-only connection with a 5-second deadline and 1 MB memory cap, wrapped with a  boundary.
3. Response composition: A second LLM pass synthesizes the query results into a concise explanation, displaying the raw SQL alongside the answer for complete transparency.

Diamonds: Predicting Price is a regression analysis project that models diamond prices from physical and quality attributes, written end to end in R. The analysis covers a dataset of ~54,000 diamonds with features including carat weight, cut grade, color grade, clarity grade, and physical dimensions (length, width, depth).

This was my earliest end-to-end data science project. I'm including it here not as a showcase of technical sophistication, but as evidence of where I started — and because the analytical thinking it required is genuinely interesting.

The full R notebook with all exploratory analysis, visualizations, and statistical modeling is available below.

View Original Analysis →

The Analysis

visualizations, and statistical modeling is available below.

View Original Analysis →

The Analysis The central challenge is that diamond price is not linear in any single feature. Carat weight has the strongest correlation with price, but two diamonds with the same carat weight can differ in price by an order of magnitude based on cut, color, and clarity. These quality grades interact with each other and with size in complex ways.

The analysis proceeded in several phases:

Exploratory data analysis: Distribution analysis revealed that carat weight clusters at round values (0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 1.5) due to market conventions, and that price distributions are right-skewed. The EDA also surfaced a data quality problem worth handling before modeling: a small number of diamonds have a recorded length, width, or depth of exactly zero, which is physically impossible. Those were converted to NAs rather than silently left in as valid measurements.

physically impossible. Those were converted to NAs rather than silently left in as valid measurements. Feature ordering: The raw quality grades (cut: Fair → Ideal, color: J → D, clarity: I1 → IF) are ordinal categories, and color ships in an order that runs best-to-worst while the others run worst-to-best. Reordering it to match makes the model coefficients read consistently across all three grades instead of one of them pointing the opposite way.

Modeling: The analysis works through four families on an 80/20 train-test split — simple and multivariate linear regression, regression decision trees (with complexity-parameter tuning), random forests, and gradient boosting machines — fitting each against both the 4 C's alone and the full feature set, and scoring every one by MAE, RMSE, and adjusted R² on the held-out data. Linear regression is the interpretable baseline; the ensembles capture the non-linear interactions more accurately at the cost of interpretability. A final comparison table ranks all of them side by side.

What I Learned

the cost of interpretability. A final comparison table ranks all of them side by side.

What I Learned The most important thing this project taught me wasn't a modeling technique — it was that fitting the model is the small part. Most of the work was upstream of it: deciding what a zero-length diamond means, getting the ordinal grades into a consistent order, and choosing which features a given model should even see. By the time the data was right, swapping between a linear model and a random forest was a few lines. That ratio has held on every project since.

between a linear model and a random forest was a few lines. That ratio has held on every project since. It also gave me an early appreciation for confounding. Plot price against cut on its own and the trend is missing — _Ideal_ diamonds don't command an obvious premium over _Fair_ ones, which is the opposite of what the grade is supposed to mean. The explanation isn't gemological, it's compositional: buyers chasing large stones tend to trade away cut quality, so the poorly cut diamonds in the data are also the biggest ones, and carat swamps the effect being measured. Any single feature plotted against price in this dataset is really showing you carat until you control for it.

Chat with Nietzsche is a conversational AI that channels Friedrich Nietzsche's philosophical voice using Retrieval-Augmented Generation over his complete written works. You can ask it about the Will to Power, Eternal Recurrence, master-slave morality, or why it thinks modern social media would have disgusted him — and get answers grounded in Nietzsche's actual writings, with source citations to the passages used.

The goal was never to make a philosophical trivia bot. It was to build a system where responses are _demonstrably_ faithful to the source material. Every answer the system produces can be traced back to real text from the 19 works in the corpus.

It began as a single-file Streamlit app. It has since been rebuilt as a full-stack application — a Next.js frontend talking to a FastAPI backend that owns the retrieval pipeline and streams tokens back to the browser.

The RAG Pipeline

FastAPI backend that owns the retrieval pipeline and streams tokens back to the browser.

The RAG Pipeline The retrieval pipeline is multi-stage, designed to maximize the quality of context passed to the LLM rather than relying on the model alone.

designed to maximize the quality of context passed to the LLM rather than relying on the model alone. 1. Question condensing: When there's conversation history, one LLM call rewrites the follow-up into a standalone question. _"What did he mean by that?"_ becomes something a search index can actually answer. The rewrite is used for retrieval only — the original message is what the model responds to. 2. Hybrid search: The condensed query hits both a FAISS semantic index (70% weight) and a BM25 keyword index (30% weight) over roughly 7,300 chunks. Semantic search handles conceptual overlap; BM25 ensures exact philosophical terms like _"Ressentiment"_ or _"Zarathustra"_ are matched precisely. 3. Fragment filtering: Candidate passages shorter than two sentences are dropped. Chunking at paragraph boundaries occasionally yields a stray heading or one-line aphorism fragment, and those crowd out passages that carry an actual argument. 4. Cross-encoder re-ranking: The survivors are re-ranked using , a cross-encoder that scores each passage against the question jointly rather than independently.

using , a cross-encoder that scores each passage against the question jointly rather than independently. This separates genuinely relevant passages from those that merely share vocabulary. The top 6 make it through. 5. Grounded generation: Those passages, the persona prompt, and the last 10 turns of history go to Groq. Temperature is set to 0.3 — low enough to suppress creative invention, high enough to avoid robotic phrasing — and tokens stream straight to the browser as they're produced.

high enough to avoid robotic phrasing — and tokens stream straight to the browser as they're produced. Technical Implementation

Corpus and chunking: All 19 works were sourced from Project Gutenberg public domain translations. Text is split at paragraph boundaries with a 1200-character target and 150-character overlap. Paragraph-based chunking preserves argumentative flow — Nietzsche's writing often builds meaning across a full paragraph, and mid-sentence splits would corrupt the context.

Embeddings:  generates 768-dimensional dense vectors for each chunk. The same model embeds user queries at inference time, ensuring semantic alignment between document and query spaces.

embeds user queries at inference time, ensuring semantic alignment between document and query spaces. Stack: FastAPI serves the retrieval pipeline and the streaming chat endpoint. FAISS and BM25 (rank-bm25) are driven directly rather than through an orchestration framework — the pipeline is specific enough that a framework's abstractions cost more than they save. Indexes are built offline and committed to the repo, so a cold start never re-embeds the corpus. The Next.js frontend never talks to the backend directly: a server-side route validates each request and proxies it, piping the token stream through unchanged.

Source citations: The UI surfaces the specific Nietzsche passages used to generate each response — title, translator, and a link to the Gutenberg source — alongside the answer. This transparency serves two purposes: it lets users verify authenticity, and it demonstrates that the retrieval pipeline found genuinely relevant context rather than hallucinating.

demonstrates that the retrieval pipeline found genuinely relevant context rather than hallucinating. Security & Gateway Architecture: The public browser talks exclusively to the Next.js origin. Its server-side  route validates the payload and proxies to the FastAPI backend presenting a shared secret header (). The backend rejects any request lacking this secret with HTTP 401 Unauthorized, preventing direct public exposure or quota exhaustion.

Deployment & CI/CD: The frontend runs on Vercel; the backend runs on Railway from a Docker image with embedding and cross-encoder models baked in so cold starts never wait on downloads. All pull requests are strictly gated in GitHub Actions: Pytest (with mocked ML models and APIs for fast, deterministic runs), Vitest with React Testing Library, Ruff, ESLint, and a Lighthouse CI budget check enforcing accessibility, best practices, and SEO.

Skills Demonstrated This project required implementing every component of an advanced RAG pipeline from first principles — no managed vector database, no off-the-shelf retrieval API. The multi-stage retrieve-filter-rerank design reflects real production RAG patterns used in enterprise retrieval systems. Rebuilding it from a Streamlit prototype into a streaming full-stack app forced the harder questions a demo never asks: what the API contract between the halves should be, where conversation state lives, and how to keep a cold start from timing out a user's first question.

This is the site you are reading. It is also the project I would point at first in a technical interview, because it is the one where I can show you numbers instead of adjectives.

The visible half is a Next.js front end. The interesting half is the chatbot in the corner: a Retrieval-Augmented Generation system that answers questions about my experience from my own resume and a written Q&A corpus, streaming responses through a FastAPI backend. Plenty of portfolios have a chatbot bolted on. What I wanted was the thing most of them skip — a way to know whether the retrieval underneath it actually works, and a gate that fails the build when it stops working.

The problem with "it seems to work"

actually works, and a gate that fails the build when it stops working.

The problem with "it seems to work" A RAG pipeline gives you a lot of knobs and very little feedback. Mine started with the parameters you would expect: a weighted blend of semantic and keyword search, ten candidates narrowed to five by a second model. Every one of those numbers was a guess. I had no answer to _"does the re-ranking stage earn its latency?"_ or _"would keyword search alone be just as good?"_, and nothing would have told me if a change to how documents get split quietly broke retrieval.

That is the situation evaluation exists for, and it is not specific to this project. Any system whose output is text has the same problem: it is always producing something plausible, so "it seems to work" is the default state whether it works or not. The only way out is to decide in advance what good means, label enough ground truth to measure it, and put the measurement somewhere it can fail.

How I decided what "good" means

truth to measure it, and put the measurement somewhere it can fail.

How I decided what "good" means The golden set is a set of questions of the kind a recruiter, hiring manager, or technical interviewer actually asks — employment history, specific technologies, project details, education, logistics. Each one is labelled with the phrases a correct answer has to be grounded in.

Labelling by _phrase_ rather than by document ID is the decision I would defend hardest. The corpus gets re-split every time I edit a source document, so any label tied to a chunk's identity is invalidated on every rebuild — the labels would rot faster than I could maintain them. Phrases survive re-chunking, which is what makes the golden set an asset rather than a chore.

The metrics are chosen for what they decide, not for what is easy to report: - hit@5 — did _any_ relevant passage reach the model? This is the one that gates the build, because it is what determines whether the system can answer at all.
- recall@5 — what share of the relevant passages made it. Reported, deliberately not gated: several questions have more than five relevant passages, so their recall is capped below 1.0 by construction and no honest threshold could ever be met. A metric you cannot set a fair threshold on is a metric you should not gate on.
- MRR and nDCG@5 — how far up the list the good passage landed, which matters because a model attends unevenly across a long context.

The thresholds sit _below_ measured performance with headroom for noise. They are floors, not targets. Tuning parameters until a floor is cleared would be fitting to my own test set, which produces numbers that look better and mean less.

The questions are split into a development portion and a held-out portion, and the table below reports the held-out one. Choices about the architecture are made against the development questions; the held-out questions are never looked at while making one. The split is assigned by hashing each question's ID, so I cannot move an inconvenient question across the line without it showing up in a test.

That last part is deliberate, and it is the only way I could find to publish results honestly over time. If I wrote the conclusion by hand, it would be a claim about one afternoon that slowly stopped being true, and I would be the last person to notice. Generating it means the page cannot flatter the architecture I happened to build: when the simplest configuration beats the elaborate one, the page says so, on its own, until I fix it.

It also means this write-up does not need rewriting when the system changes. The numbers move, the verdict follows them, and the prose around it stays true because it never claimed to know the answer.

What the evaluation changed

Metrics are only worth collecting if they alter what you build. This is the running record of what the harness found and what I did about it — appended to, never rewritten.

Two of those entries share a pattern I found useful to learn: the code looked correct, every component behaved exactly as specified, every test passed, and nothing was going to surface the problem except a number moving. Unit tests tell you the parts do what you said; only measurement tells you the system does what you meant.

tests tell you the parts do what you said; only measurement tells you the system does what you meant. The third one is the one I would actually want to be asked about. I built a hybrid retrieval pipeline — semantic search fused with keyword search, then a cross-encoder re-ranking the candidates — because that is the architecture you build when you are demonstrating that you can build it. The evaluation said plain keyword search beat it on every metric. The tempting response was to retune the fusion weights until the numbers came back, and that would have been the wrong experiment: under the fusion formula I was using, tuning the semantic weight toward zero and switching the semantic stage off are the same experiment, so "find the optimal ratio" would have been a slower path to the answer I already had, ending in a magic constant with nothing behind it. So I ran the experiment that actually asked the question — keyword candidates fed straight to the re-ranker, no semantic stage at all — and it beat the full pipeline. Then the re-ranker failed the same test against keyword search alone.

and it beat the full pipeline. Then the re-ranker failed the same test against keyword search alone. The fix was to delete the architecture. Production retrieval is now keyword search and nothing else, which cut the backend from 87 production dependencies to 40 and the deployed container image from 17.2GB to 544MB. Most of that was not the model weights — it was , which the embedding library pulls in, and whose default Linux wheels ship the NVIDIA CUDA runtime into a container that has no GPU. I had been deploying several gigabytes of GPU libraries to serve keyword search, and nothing was ever going to tell me that except deciding the stage that needed them had not earned its place. Cheaper _and_ better is a stronger result than a tuned constant, and it is not the result I wanted when I started. Every deleted stage is still measured as a configuration on every run, because this corpus is written as anticipated questions and answers — the exact condition that flatters keyword matching — and I expect that to stop being true as the corpus grows.

When it does, I want the harness to be what tells me, not a rebuild from scratch. Engineering around it

The eval is a CI gate, not a notebook. It runs on every backend change and fails the build if the shipped configuration drops below its floor, so retrieval quality cannot regress silently between commits. The other configurations are measured and published for comparison but not gated: a floor exists to stop a change degrading what a visitor is served, and nothing is served by a configuration production does not run. Because production is now keyword-only, the gate itself runs in seconds and needs no model weights at all.

Actions, so  reproduces the PR gates exactly — no drift between what passes locally and what passes in CI. One gate is there because of a specific mistake. My resume is a source document for the index, and it carried my home address and phone number, which meant the chatbot would read them back to anyone who asked. The fix was three-layered: strip it at the source, redact it during the index build as a backstop, and add a regression test that fails the build if a phone number or street address ever appears in the committed index again. The redaction and the detection are deliberately asymmetric — the redactor is precise, because rewriting the corpus silently means a false positive destroys real content unnoticed, while the test guard casts a wide net, because its only power is to fail a build and a false positive there costs one glance from me.

What I am not claiming The corpus is small, and much of it is written as anticipated questions with answers — which is exactly the condition that favours keyword matching over semantic search. Relevance is also labelled by exact phrase presence, which is close to what keyword ranking measures. Every configuration is scored against identical labels, so the comparison is internally fair, but any conclusion it supports is about _this_ corpus rather than about retrieval in general.

That bias cuts directly against the conclusion I drew from it, which is why the retired configurations are still measured rather than deleted from the harness: the result that told me to remove them is the same result I expect to reverse as the corpus grows past the point where the questions and the documents share vocabulary.

Skills Demonstrated

The RAG pipeline is the part that looks impressive. The evaluation suite is the part that matters, and it is the difference between an engineer who assembles components and one who can tell you whether the assembly works.

difference between an engineer who assembles components and one who can tell you whether the assembly works. This project shows I can define what "good" means for a system whose output is text, label ground truth in a form that survives the corpus changing underneath it, hold a portion of it back so published numbers are not tuned numbers, choose metrics for what they decide rather than what is easy to report, wire the result into CI as a gate rather than a report — and build the publishing path so that the conclusions stay honest as the system evolves, including the time the measurement contradicted the architecture I had already built and the right answer was to delete it.
